title: Patching Up Circuit Learning on Images
claim: Our approach beats the independence-assuming baseline on speed, memory, compute and accuracy across many architectures, and scales where the baseline cannot.
layout: 3 scatter panels in a row, shared y-axis, dashed arrows from baseline to ours
description: Three side-by-side scatter plots share a y-axis, test bits-per-dimension (bpd), which runs from about 4.8 to 5.4. The x-axes are average step time in seconds, max GPU memory in GB, and FLOPs, all on log scales. Each marker shape (diamond, square, cross, triangles, plus, circle, star) is one PC architecture. Blue markers mark the baseline (IPA/independent patches) and orange markers mark RePA. Dashed gray arrows run from each blue marker to its orange counterpart. In the time and memory panels the arrows mostly point left and down, so RePA is faster, smaller and lower in bpd. In the FLOPs panel the arrows mostly point straight down. Some orange markers have no blue partner. A legend sits in the top-right of the first panel. The eye goes first to the arrows and the blue-to-orange color shift.
caption: \repa delivers faster, smaller and more accurate circuits compared to PCs that assume patch independence (\indepatch). This is shown here in terms of average step time (seconds), GPU memory, FLOPs and bpd (i.e. normalized negative log-likelihoods) on ImageNet32 for several tensorized PC architectures. \repa markers (yellow) that have no corresponding \indepatch markers (blue) are those for which \indepatch could not be trained on 40GB GPUs in under 2 days. See [ref] for similar trends on CelebA and ImageNet64 and the precise PC configuration associated to each marker.
abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) have emerged as generative models guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference. However, tractability comes at the price of larger model sizes than in other generative models. As such, to scale PCs to high-dimensional data such as images, previous work has devised several parameter sharing techniques as well as fast evaluation protocols that consider learning PCs on independent image patches. In this work, we revisit this practice to highlight a surprising learnability issue: models that assume independence counterintuitively can yield better likelihoods than models that do not. To break this apparent bottleneck and to scale PCs further, we introduce a recursive parameter sharing construction (RePA) that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. We show empirically that RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods.Inspired by these results, we further generalize the approach to data modalities that do not inherently exhibit patch-structure (NoPA), such as tabular data, showing similar efficiency improvements, with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality on seven tabular datasets. Code available at https://github.com/april-tools/RePA.
